Battle of Gettysburg. From July first to third, eighteen sixty-three, the largest and most significant battle of the American Civil War unfolded in and around the town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The Union Army of the Potomac, commanded by Major General George Meade, defeated General Robert E. Lee's Confederate Army of Northern Virginia in a three-day engagement that marked a turning point in the war. Approximately fifty thousand soldiers were killed, wounded, or missing. The battle effectively ended Lee's invasion of the North and shattered the myth of Southern invincibility, giving the Union decisive strategic momentum.

Lee sought to invade Pennsylvania to draw Union forces away from the South and gain a major victory on Northern soil that might sway European powers toward Confederate recognition. Meade assumed command of the Union forces only days before the battle and was initially unaware of Lee's exact position. The armies collided by accident when Confederate units searching for supplies encountered Union cavalry on July first.

Union forces held the high ground—Cemetery Ridge and Culp's Hill—and repulsed Confederate assaults on all three days despite being initially outnumbered. Pickett's Charge on July third was Lee's last major assault. Thirteen thousand Confederate infantry crossed open ground toward the Union center and were decimated by artillery and rifle fire. Fewer than half returned to Confederate lines. The Union cavalry, under Jeb Stuart, arrived late and failed to strike Meade's rear, denying Lee a crucial advantage.

Lee retreated to Virginia on July fourth, ending his invasion. Casualties were catastrophic. The Union lost approximately twenty-three thousand soldiers. The Confederacy lost approximately twenty-eight thousand. The South could not replace these losses. The victory boosted Northern morale and prompted Lincoln to issue the Emancipation Proclamation to take effect in January.

Gettysburg stands as the hinge upon which the Civil War turned. Before it, the Confederacy seemed capable of winning through persistence and superior generalship. After it, the Union's numerical and industrial advantage became insurmountable. The battle's tactical lessons—entrenchment, defensive positioning, the cost of frontal assault against prepared positions—echoed through World War I. In American memory, Gettysburg became the crucible of national survival. Lincoln's address there in November eighteen sixty-three reframed the war not as a constitutional conflict but as a test of whether a democratic nation could endure.
